newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bourse head slams gov't-union labor deal.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bourse head slams gov't-union labor deal.

text.p: The president of Buenos Aires stock exchange on Sunday blasted a government-union labour reform deal which had raised hopes of averting a looming general strike.
"In principle it (the deal) is quite far from the points we had agreed upon at the Group of Eight (g8)" main business lobbies, Julio Macchi, an influential business leader.

Macchi told Radio America the G8 wanted all special labor concessions for some unions abolished, wheras the deal announced Friday by the government and the CGT main union federation "maintains the special statutes."
The CGT threatens to launch a strike in May unless unions, the government and the business sector agree on labour reforms.

Three-way talks between the G8, the CGT and the government broke down in March over President Carlos Menem's plans to reform labor legislation as requested by the International Monetary Fund and the business community.
Cabinet chief Jorge Rodriguez Saturday called the agreement in principle a "very positive" development which should help reduce unemployment now standing at 17.3 percent.

"We hope that the agreements between government and unions will have the support of the business sector so that we can make headway in labor legislation modernization, which is a very important step towards improving work access for Argentines," he told a local radio station.
The CGT has said that if the G8 approved of the pact it might ditch its plans to call for a general strike sometime this month.
Macchi made clear his was only a preliminary reading and that the agreement would be scrutinized by G8 technicians. But he insisted some points represented "a major step back."
On Saturday, the hard-line Argentine Workers Center (CTA) called the accord, which reportedly includes an agreement to cut severance payment by 30 percent, unacceptable.
"It is inadmissible that such a deal would not tackle the problem of unemployment," it said in a press release.

And the Business Unity Council of Buenos Aires, which gropus small entreprises in Argentina's main industrial belt, complained it was shut out of the talks despite representing "the main sources of jobs in the country."

The government proposes swapping lump sum severance for unemployment insurance and allowing workers to make salary and labor condition deals directly with employers with no centralized union intervention. It is also pushing for a complete deregulation of the union-controlled private health system. ((--David Haskel, Buenos Aires Newsroom +541 318-0652))
